title: Deconstructing the Monolith - Shopify
summary: Shopify explains why it chose a modular monolith over microservices: the unbounded monolith had become fragile and hard to learn, services would add pipelines and network cost, so it reorganised by domain and enforced boundaries with tooling.

assertions.quote: Making a seemingly innocuous change could trigger a cascade of unrelated test failures.

verdicts.note: Coupling-defect and comprehension research supports it; Shopify's developer survey is a single case.

assertions.quote: no architecture is often the best architecture in the early days of a system
A modular monolith is a system where all of the code powers a single application and there are strictly enforced boundaries between different domains.
communicating between services means crossing the network, which adds latency and decreases reliability with every call
large refactors across multiple services can be tedious, requiring changes across all dependent services and coordinating deploys
Microservices surged in popularity in recent years and were touted as the end-all solution to all of the problems arising from monoliths.
Designing a complex system of microservices before you have domain expertise is a risky move that too many software projects fall into.
re-organize it by real-world concepts (like orders, shipping, inventory, and billing), in an attempt to make it easier to locate code

verdicts.note: Package-by-feature is widely recommended; the evidence is practitioner experience.

assertions.quote: in the early stages of most applications you can move very quickly with little design

verdicts.note: Fowler's design stamina hypothesis is a hypothesis; consistent with debt-payoff reasoning.
